paras: The arrest and beating of E. C. and John Perdue took place near Muscogee, Escambia County, Florida, on August 22, 1910, when Deputy Sheriff S. T. Andrews arrested the two Black men on a charge of attempted assault on a white woman and clubbed one with his pistol. Sheriff Van Pelt later said the woman had told Andrews the men were not her assailants; he dismissed the deputy, released the men, and arrested Andrews on a warrant sworn out by their father. A mob reportedly formed to take the men from jail, and the Pensacola press treated Andrews's conduct as incitement.

At the time, the Pensacola county jail also held Keyser Brown, a Black man charged with murdering Marshal Smith of Bay Minette, Alabama. On Sunday night, August 21, Mrs. Julia Middleton reported that a man had entered her house near Muscogee, seized her and tried to choke her, fleeing when she screamed and small boys or neighbors came running. Two men later approached a house where Miss Lena Lowry, eighteen, drove them off with pistols and gave the description used in the search.

Late on the afternoon of Monday, August 22, Andrews and another deputy arrested two men named Perdue near McKinnon's creek. Andrews told the Pensacola Journal that Mrs. Middleton identified E. R. [E. C.] Purdue and that when the man broke for liberty he clubbed him with his pistol, cutting his scalp so badly it had to be sewed. The other man collapsed in his cell in what the paper called a "jail fit."

Sheriff Van Pelt brought the Perdues into Pensacola about 7:30 that evening, along with Keyser Brown, and there was some excitement in the streets. At the jail, the sheriff said, Andrews told the crowd, "I'm the bully that can straddle them—they're the right negroes, boys," then went down Palafox street telling people the men had been identified.

On the night of August 23 the sheriff received word from Muscogee that a mob of "countrymen" had formed to come to the city and take the two Perdues from the jail. He moved them by closed carriage to a hiding place and, with Police Chief Sanders, guarded the jail until daylight, but no mob arrived.

On August 23 Sheriff Van Pelt revoked Andrews's commission, calling his statements "a tissue of falsehoods" and saying Mrs. Middleton had "very emphatically" told Andrews the men were not the ones. He said the Perdues were in no condition to leave the jail and that he feared one might not leave it alive. With no evidence against them, he released them.

On August 27 the sheriff arrested Andrews for assault and battery on a warrant sworn out by the Perdues' father, who was the prosecutor; Andrews gave a $200 bond. The father's charge was that Andrews beat the men after they had been handcuffed and after the woman had said they were not the right parties, and that one fell unconscious on reaching the jail. No report of a trial or its outcome was found.

The Montgomery Advertiser's first Pensacola special, headed "FOILS NEGROES; POSSE PURSUES," presented the men as the assailants, saying E. C. Perdue "was wounded, when he resisted arrest" and that both had been identified. A wire story in the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Washington Evening Star gave the charge and the Lowry episode without the beating.

The Pensacola Journal reversed course within a day, headlining Andrews's dismissal and reporting that many took his conduct as "nothing short of attempt to start a race riot." The Advertiser followed with the threatened mob and Andrews's arrest, and on September 4 the Journal reprinted a Marianna Times-Courier editorial saying Andrews had "brutally handled" the men without cause and should have been jailed for exciting "mob violence."

The first reports, drawn from Andrews, said Mrs. Middleton identified one or both men; the sheriff, after inquiry, said she told Andrews they were not the ones. Andrews's version that Perdue was struck while breaking away also conflicts with the father's charge that the men were beaten in handcuffs; the sheriff's account and the release support the later version.

reader.title: Arrest and beating of E. C. and John Perdue
bases: A deputy sheriff arrested two Black men on an assault charge and beat one with his pistol (A4, A8, A10, A11); a mob that reportedly set out to take them from jail never arrived (A7, A9).

The arrest and the pistol beating are reported independently by the Pensacola Journal from Andrews's own account and the sheriff's (A4, A8, A11) and by Montgomery Advertiser specials (A2, A10); the identification and the cause of the injury are contested (A2, A4 vs. A8, A10).

framing.detail: The first Montgomery Advertiser report ran under 'FOILS NEGROES; POSSE PURSUES' and 'BRAVE GIRL DRIVES BLACKS AWAY,' treated the men as the assailants and called the wound the result of resisting arrest.
The wire story ('TWO NEGROES ARE CAUGHT BY SHERIFF'; 'FACE SERIOUS CHARGES.') gave only the charge and the Lowry pistol episode.
The Pensacola Journal headlined Andrews's discharge, quoted the sheriff calling his statements falsehoods, and reported that many took his conduct as an attempt to start a race riot.
A Marianna Times-Courier editorial reprinted in the Journal said Andrews 'brutally handled' the men without cause and should have been jailed for exciting mob violence.
